extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, judges, law professors, and advanced law students (U.S. patent litigation audience)
extracted.subtask_description: Standards and procedural criteria for analyzing and resolving patent validity issues (anticipation, obviousness, enablement, indefiniteness, eligibility) across pleading, summary judgment, trial, and appeal in U.S. federal courts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: "[The party alleging invalidity] met its burden of showing invalidity by clear and convincing evidence."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Federal Circuit/Supreme Court precedent stressing that invalidity must be proven by clear and convincing evidence at trial; appellate review must account for that burden when assessing whether jury verdicts are supported by substantial evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate review of jury obviousness verdicts
rubrics_metrics.description: In reviewing a jury’s obviousness verdict, courts: first presume that the jury resolved the underlying factual disputes in favor of the verdict winner and leave those presumed findings undisturbed if supported by substantial evidence; second, examine the legal conclusion de novo in light of the presumed jury fact findings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quoted formulation (e.g., Ultratec v. Sorenson; Cir. Check v. QXQ). Explains the two-step appellate approach: deferential review of presumed factual findings (substantial evidence) then de novo review of the legal conclusion of obviousness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of nonobviousness: fact vs law vs mixed
rubrics_metrics.description: Nonobviousness has been treated sometimes as a question of fact (for the jury), sometimes a question of law (for the judge), and increasingly by some courts as a 'mixed question of law and fact.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Describes the doctrinal confusion and practical consequences (litigation over jury instructions, verdict forms, duplicative judge/jury decisions, uncertainty over appellate deference). Cites Federal Circuit cases and commentary finding varied approaches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Thesis: Treat patent validity as a mixed question of law and fact
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts should treat all grounds of patent validity as ultimately presenting mixed questions of law and fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Normative proposal: calling validity a mixed question would resolve doctrine confusion, clarify jury role, appellate deference, review of PTO actions, and application of the statutory presumption of validity. Explains mapping to U.S. Bank three-step framework.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three-step analytic framework (U.S. Bank mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Step 1: settle on the legal test; Step 2: make findings of basic/historical fact; Step 3: determine whether the facts found satisfy the legal test (the mixed question).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied examples: §102 anticipation (elements in single reference), §103 nonobviousness (would it be obvious to a person of ordinary skill), §112 enablement (recreate without undue experimentation), §101 eligibility (Mayo/Alice two-step). Emphasizes that step three is the ultimate validity determination and should be seen as mixed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal-test identification for major doctrines
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples of the legal tests courts must select: for §102: Were all elements disclosed in a single prior art reference?; for §103: Would the invention have been obvious to a person of ordinary skill?; for §112 (enablement): Could a person of ordinary skill recreate the invention without undue experimentation?; for §101: the Mayo/Alice two-step eligibility framework.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are 'purely legal' questions that should be decided by the judge and reviewed de novo as to legal content, but they do not resolve the ultimate validity question without the factual record.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleading-stage resolution conditions for validity
rubrics_metrics.description: A court may decide validity at the pre-discovery pleading stage only when (1) the patentee cannot plausibly allege that its patent satisfies the legal requirements of patentability and (2) the patent’s invalidity is clear based on materials a court may properly consider on a pleading-stage motion (the complaint, the patent itself, and other materials whose veracity is incontrovertible and subject to judicial notice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draws on Ashcroft v. Iqbal/Twombly pleading standards and Rule 12(b)(6) practice: defenses apparent on the face of the complaint may justify dismissal. Emphasizes the court may only consider certain intrinsic or judicially-noticeable public records at this stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intrinsic-record dismissal for eligibility (§101)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent eligibility can be dismissed at the pleading stage when the intrinsic record makes clear the claim is directed to an abstract idea or natural phenomenon and employs only conventional technology.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides case examples (BSG Tech; Cleveland Clinic; Chamberlain) where intrinsic evidence made ineligibility obvious. Contrasts with cases where factual allegations about unconventionality should be credited and the case permitted to proceed to discovery (Aatrix tension).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation (§102) pleading-stage rule when prior art is judicially noticeable
rubrics_metrics.description: Anticipation can be resolved on the pleadings when all elements of the claim are plainly disclosed in a prior art document that is subject to judicial notice (e.g., a prior art patent), because that public record's veracity cannot be controverted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: But dismissal is inappropriate when claim construction or interpretation of the prior art is plausibly disputed; recasting anticipation as a mixed question clarifies that pleading-stage resolution is sometimes appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Indefiniteness (§112(b)) as mixed question and when resolvable on pleadings
rubrics_metrics.description: Indefiniteness stems from §112(b) requiring claims to 'particularly point[] out and distinctly claim[]' the invention; a patent is indefinite if it 'fail[s] to inform, with reasonable certainty, those skilled in the art about the scope of the invention.' Determining indefiniteness involves claim construction and thus is properly characterized as a mixed question of law and fact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Indefiniteness can be decided at the pleading stage when the judge can confidently determine impermissible vagueness based on the intrinsic record (patent, specification, prosecution history). If extrinsic evidence is needed, decision should be postponed. Argues that judges, not juries, should decide indefiniteness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Role of intrinsic versus extrinsic evidence in validity determinations
rubrics_metrics.description: Intrinsic evidence (the patent specification, claims, prosecution history) can be evaluated as a matter of law and may suffice for early dismissal in clear cases; extrinsic evidence (prior art not judicially noticeable, expert testimony about a person of ordinary skill, etc.) raises factual disputes requiring further proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: enablement/nonobviousness usually require extrinsic evidence and are harder to resolve on pleadings; eligibility, anticipation, and indefiniteness sometimes resolve on intrinsic record. Emphasizes when factual disputes exist, dismissal is inappropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rule 12(b)(6) and affirmative defenses of invalidity
rubrics_metrics.description: An affirmative defense (like invalidity) can form the basis for dismissal under Rule 12(b)(6) if it is clearly indicated on the face of the plaintiff’s pleadings and appears on the face of the pleading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites Rule 12(b)(6) doctrine and 5B WRIGHT ET AL.: dismissal is appropriate where the applicability of the defense is clearly indicated by the complaint and supporting documents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of special interrogatories and jury instructions to preserve factual findings
rubrics_metrics.description: When a jury is asked to determine obviousness, it is preferred that the jury be provided with special interrogatories regarding the Graham factors relevant to the case so that the jury’s underlying factual findings are known.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patent Case Management Judicial Guide recommends special interrogatories; N.D. Cal. model jury instructions provide for jury answers to aid judge in deciding ultimate legal question of obviousness and for advisory verdict situations. This practice helps appellate review by revealing underlying factual determinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences for summary judgment and the jury's role
rubrics_metrics.description: Viewing patent validity as a mixed question could make district judges more willing to decide validity at summary judgment and would, in effect, remove the jury from most disputes over patent validity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Argues that with no jury trial anticipated, judges may be more willing to grant summary judgment; empirical evidence shows summary judgment on validity is hard to win because judges often treat technologically complex inquiries as factual disputes better suited for jury resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appellate deference and review post-mixed-question framing
rubrics_metrics.description: Treating validity as a mixed question would clarify the appropriate appellate deference: factual findings should be reviewed deferentially (clear error/substantial evidence), pure legal content de novo, and the ultimate mixed question recognized as the application of legal doctrine to case-specific facts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains current confusion (some courts treating ultimate validity as law; others giving deference) and suggests mixed-question framing would better allocate standards of review and remove doctrinal formalism.
